kick.e: From Middle English kyken (“to strike out with the foot”), from Old Norse kikna (“to sink at the knees”) and keikja (“to bend backwards”) (compare Old Norse keikr (“bent backwards, the belly jutting forward”)), from Proto-Germanic *kaikaz (“bent backwards”), of uncertain origin.
kick.g: To strike or hit with the foot or other extremity of the leg.

kid.e: From Middle English kide, from Old Norse kið (“young goat”), from Proto-Germanic *kidją, *kittīną (“goatling, kid”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gʰaydn-, *ǵʰaydn- (“goat”) or Proto-Indo-European *gidʰ- (“kid, goatling, little goat”). The sense of child has been in use since the 1590s as slang, and since the 1840s in informal use.
kid.g: A child, adolescent, or (loosely) a young adult.

kid.e: Of uncertain origin. Possibly from Middle English *kidde, from Old English *cydde (“pouch, belly”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuddijā, derived from or related to Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“bag, sack, pod, shell, husk”).
kid.g: A seed pod, usually of a leguminous plant.

kidnap.e: From kid + nap (“to nab; to grab”). Originally Thieves' cant, referring to the practice of stealing children and shipping them to colonies or plantations as laborers.
kidnap.g: To seize or detain (a person) unlawfully and transport or conceal them, sometimes for ransom.

kidney.e: From Middle English kideney, kydeney, alteration of earlier kidenere (“kidney”) after ey (“egg”), of obscure origin and formation. Probably a compound consisting of Middle English *kidde (“sack”) + Middle English nere (“kidney”). The first element would be from Old English *cydde (“sack, scrotum”).
kidney.g: An organ in the body that filters the blood, producing urine.

kill.e: From Middle English killen, kyllen, cüllen (“to strike, beat, cut”), of obscure origin. Perhaps from unattested Old English *cyllan, from Proto-West Germanic *kwulljan, from Proto-Germanic *kwuljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- (“to throw, hit, hurt by throwing”). Or, possibly a variant of Old English cwellan (“to kill, murder, execute”) (see quell).
kill.g: To put to death; to extinguish the life of.

kill.e: Borrowing from Dutch kil (formerly spelled kill), from Middle Dutch kille, from Old Dutch *killa, from Proto-West Germanic *killjā, from Proto-Germanic *kiljǭ (“fissure, slit; a type of stream, creek, channel”). Most place names with kill were derived entirely in Dutch, but many have been subsequently calqued into English or anglicized by folk etymology.
kill.g: A creek or stream; (more loosely) any watercourse, such as a channel or arm of the sea.

killer.e: From Middle English killer, kyller. By surface analysis, kill + -er.
killer.g: One who or that which kills.

killing.e: From Middle English kyllyng; equivalent to kill + -ing.
killing.g: That literally deprives of life; lethal, deadly, fatal.

kiln.e: From Middle English kilne, from Old English cyln, cylen, cylin (“large oven, kiln”), from Latin culīna (“kitchen, kitchen stove”). Middle English -ln(e) usually becomes modern -ll as in mill. The pronunciation /kɪln/ may be based on dialects in which this simplification did not take place, but it must have been at least reinforced by spelling pronunciation.
kiln.g: An oven or furnace or a heated chamber, for the purpose of hardening, burning, calcining or drying anything; for example, firing ceramics, c

kin.e: From Middle English kyn, from Old English cynn (“kind, sort, rank”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuni, from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“race, generation, descent”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₁yom, from *ǵenh₁- (“to produce”).
Borrowed from Mandarin 琴 (qín), from a non-palatal dialect akin to Peking; or less likely, from Japanese 琴 (kin).
kin.g: Alternative form of qin (“Chinese string instrument”).

kind.e: From Middle English kynde, kinde, from Old English cynd, ġecynd (“inherent nature, disposition, kind, gender, generation, race”), from Proto-West Germanic *kundi, from Proto-Germanic *kinþiz, related to Proto-Germanic *kunją (“race, kin”) and Old English cennan (“to bear, give birth”).
kind.g: A type, race or category; a group of entities that have common characteristics such that they may be grouped together.

kind.e: From Middle English kynde, kinde, from Old English cynde, ġecynde (“innate, natural, native”), from Old English cynd, ġecynd (“nature, kind”).
kind.g: Having a benevolent, courteous, friendly, generous, gentle, liberal, sympathetic, or warm-hearted nature or disposition, marked by considera

kindle.e: From Middle English kyndelen, from Old Norse kynda (“to inflame”), from Proto-Germanic *kundijaną.
kindle.g: To start (a fire) or light (a torch, a match, coals, etc.).

kindle.e: From Middle English kyndel, from kynde + -el.
kindle.g: A group, usually a litter, of kittens, or sometimes cats more generally.

kindly.e: From Middle English kyndely, kyndeliche, from Old English cyndelīċ (“natural, kindly”); equivalent to kind + -ly.
kindly.g: Having a kind personality; kind, warm-hearted, sympathetic.

kindly.e: From Middle English kyndely, kyndly, kyndeliche, from Old English ġecyndelīċe, equivalent to kind + -ly.
kindly.g: In a kind manner, out of kindness.

kindness.e: From Middle English kyndenesse, equivalent to kind + -ness.

kindred.e: From Middle English kyndrede, from older kynrede (“kindred”), from Old English *cynrēd, *cynrǣden (“kindred, family, stock”), from cynn (“kind, kin, lineage”) + -rǣden (“condition, state”). Equivalent to kin + -red, see these. The -d- is epenthetic between a nasal and a liquid (as e.g. in spindle).
kindred.g: Distant and close relatives, collectively; kin.

kine.e: From Middle English kyn, kyne, equivalent to ky + -en (plural ending), a double plural.

king.e: From Middle English king, kyng, kynge, from Old English cening, cing, cining, cuning, cyncg, cyneg, cyng, cyngc, cynig, cyning, king, kining, kuning, kyning, kyningc (“king”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuning, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz, *kunungaz (“king”), from *kunją (“clan, family, kin”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to produce; to beget”).
king.g: A male monarch; a man who heads a monarchy; in an absolute monarchy, the supreme ruler of his nation.

kingly.e: From Middle English kyngly, from Old English *cyninglīċ (“kingly, royal”), equivalent to king + -ly.
kingly.g: Of or belonging to a king or kings; exercised by a king.

kingly.e: From Middle English kyngly, from Old English *cyninglīċe (“kingly, royally”), equivalent to king + -ly.

kinsfolk.e: From Middle English kynsefolke, after kynnesman (modern English kinsman), equivalent to kin + -s- + folk.

kinsman.e: From Middle English kynnesman, equivalent to kin + -s- + -man.

kinswoman.e: From Middle English kynneswomman; equivalent to kin + -s- + -woman.

kiss.e: From Middle English kissen, kussen, from Old English cyssan (“to kiss”), from Proto-West Germanic *kussijan, from Proto-Germanic *kussijaną (“to kiss”).
kiss.g: To touch with the lips or press the lips against, usually to show love or affection or passion, or as part of a greeting.

kiss.e: From Middle English kis, kys, kus, forms of cos influenced by kissen, from Old English coss, from Proto-West Germanic *koss, from Proto-Germanic *kussaz.
kiss.g: A touch with the lips, usually to express love or affection, or as a greeting.

kissing.e: From Middle English kissynge, cussinde, from Old English cyssende, from Proto-West Germanic *kussijandī, from Proto-Germanic *kussijandz, equivalent to kiss + -ing.
kissing.g: That kisses; engaged in a kiss or kissing.

kit.e: From Middle English kyt, kytt, kytte, from Middle Dutch kitte (“a wooden vessel made of hooped staves”). The further etymology is unknown. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *kitjō-, *kut-, which would be related to the root of Dutch kot (“ramshackle house”), itself of non-Indo-European origin.
kit.g: A circular wooden vessel, made of hooped staves.

kit.e: From the 16th century, spelled kytte, kitt. From the 19th century also extended to other young animals (beaver, fox, mink, muskrat, etc.), and to a species of small fox (kit fox). Later usage (for other animals) perhaps influenced by chit.

kitchen.e: From Middle English kichene, kichen, from Old English cyċen, cyċene, from Proto-West Germanic *kukinā, a borrowing from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna (“kitchen; cuisine”), from coquō (“to cook”), from Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- (“to cook, become ripe”). In other languages, the cognate term often refers both to the room and the type of cooking.
kitchen.g: A room or area for preparing food.

kite.e: The English word is cognate with Scots kyt, kyte (“kite; bird of prey”), Middle High German kiuzelīn, kützlīn (“owling”) (modern German Kauz (“owl”)). Possibly a doublet of coot. Sense 3 (“lightweight toy”) is from the fact that it hovers in the air like the bird.
kite.g: A bird of prey of the family Accipitridae.

kite.e: Uncertain; possibly: from Middle English kit, kitte (“wooden bucket or tub; (figuratively) belly”), possibly from Middle Dutch kitte (“wooden vessel of hooped staves”) (modern Dutch kit (“metal can used mainly for coal”)), further etymology unknown; or from Old Norse kýta (“bag, stomach (of a fish)”), from Proto-Germanic *kūtiz.
